turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: His misfortunes! Do not imagine me so deficient in discretion as to allude to any communications which have been made to me in strictness of confidence. I am not ashamed to acknowledge that I feel, and have felt, a more than common interest in Mr. Wickham's welfare. The resemblance of personal manners which had for so many years attracted my regard, the near intimacy which had for several winters distinguished him from all his companions, the dependent situation of his father during the latter part of his life, and the attachment of Mr. Darcy’s father to his family, have united to make me feel for Mr. Wickham with some share of that partiality which a longer acquaintance would have increased.

turns.speaker: Mr. Darcy
turns.text: Your partiality towards Mr. Wickham is evident, yet it is I who must declare my feelings towards you, Miss Elizabeth. Despite my pride, I find myself compelled to acknowledge my admiration and love for you.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: Mr. Darcy, your sudden declaration astonishes me. I have never even considered myself your equal in society or fortune, and I certainly never expected to hear such a confession from you.

turns.speaker: Mr. Darcy
turns.text: Indeed, Miss Elizabeth, the disparity between us is acknowledged by all, yet it does not diminish the sincerity of my feelings. I must confess that my pride has often been my own undoing, and I regret the pain it has caused you.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: Mr. Darcy, your words astonish me. I have long perceived your pride and your disdain for those beneath you in station. Such feelings cannot be overcome by a mere declaration of love.

turns.speaker: Mr. Darcy
turns.text: I am aware of the perception of my pride, Elizabeth, and I have struggled against it. Yet, my heart cannot be controlled as easily as my tongue, and it is my heart that now compels me to speak.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: Mr. Darcy, your perception of my feelings must be far from reality. Your pride has often been a barrier between us, and it will take more than a declaration to convince me of a change of heart.

turns.speaker: Mr. Darcy
turns.text: Elizabeth, your assessment of my character is not entirely unfounded, but I assure you that my heart has changed. My pride has indeed been my greatest obstacle, but it is not the entirety of who I am.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: Mr. Darcy, your words do touch upon my heart, but they also raise questions that cannot be easily dismissed. Your pride has wounded those I hold dear, and it will take more than words to heal the wounds you have caused.

turns.speaker: Mr. Darcy
turns.text: I understand the depth of the wounds I have inflicted, Elizabeth, and I am prepared to earn back your trust and the trust of those you hold dear. My pride has been my downfall, but I am willing to change.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: Mr. Darcy, your words are sincere, but your actions have spoken louder than your words ever could. I have witnessed your pride in action, and it is not easily forgotten.

turns.speaker: Mr. Darcy
turns.text: Elizabeth, your criticisms are just and I acknowledge them. My actions have been the true measure of my character, and I now see the necessity to prove my sincerity through deeds, not merely words.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: Mr. Darcy, your recognition of your faults is a start, but it is the steps you take to correct them that will truly matter.

turns.speaker: Mr. Darcy
turns.text: Elizabeth, I comprehend the gravity of the task before me. My actions will demonstrate my commitment to change.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: Mr. Darcy, your intentions now may be clear, but your past actions have left a deep impression. I shall observe your conduct closely.

turns.speaker: Mr. Darcy
turns.text: I am aware of the burden I must bear. My past shall not dictate my future. I shall prove my sincerity through my actions, Elizabeth.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: Mr. Darcy, your words are earnest, but your actions will be the true measure of your sincerity. I shall watch for them with great interest.

turns.speaker: Mr. Darcy
turns.text: I understand, Elizabeth. My past actions have indeed caused you great pain, and it is my duty to earn back your trust through my conduct.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: Mr. Darcy, I have no doubt that your words are sincere now, but actions will indeed speak louder than words. I shall be watching closely.

turns.speaker: Mr. Darcy
turns.text: I shall strive to earn your regard, Elizabeth. My actions shall reflect the sincerity of my words.

opening.speaker: Mr. Darcy
opening.text: In vain have I struggled. It will not do. My feelings will not be repressed. You must allow me to tell you how ardently I admire and love you.

opening.speaker: Elizabeth
opening.text: In such cases as this, it is, I believe, the established mode to express a sense of obligation for the sentiments avowed, however unequally they may be returned. It is natural that obligation should be felt, and if I could feel gratitude, I would now thank you. But I cannot--I have never desired your good opinion, and you have certainly bestowed it most unwillingly. I am sorry to have occasioned pain to anyone. It has been most unconsciously done, however, and I hope will be of short duration. The feelings which you tell me have long prevented the acknowledgment of your regard can have little difficulty in overcoming it after this explanation.

opening.speaker: Mr. Darcy
opening.text: And this is all the reply which I am to have the honour of expecting! I might, perhaps, wish to be informed why, with so little endeavour at civility, I am thus rejected. But it is of small importance.

opening.speaker: Elizabeth
opening.text: I might as well inquire, why, with so evident a design of offending and insulting me, you chose to tell me that you liked me against your will, against your reason, and even against your character? Was not this some excuse for incivility, if I was uncivil? But I have other provocations. You know I have. Had not my own feelings decided against you, had they been indifferent, or had they even been favourable, do you think that any consideration would tempt me to accept the man who has been the means of ruining, perhaps for ever, the happiness of a most beloved sister?

opening.speaker: Elizabeth
opening.text: I have every reason in the world to think ill of you. No motive can excuse the unjust and ungenerous part you acted there. You dare not, you cannot deny that you have been the principal, if not the only means of dividing them from each other, of exposing one to the censure of the world for caprice and instability, the other to its derision for disappointed hopes, and involving them both in misery of the acutest kind.

opening.speaker: Elizabeth
opening.text: But it is not merely this affair, on which my dislike is founded. Long before it had taken place, my opinion of you was decided. Your character was unfolded in the recital which I received many months ago from Mr. Wickham. On this subject, what can you have to say? In what imaginary act of friendship can you here defend yourself? or under what misrepresentation can you here impose upon others?

opening.speaker: Mr. Darcy
opening.text: You take an eager interest in that gentleman’s concerns

opening.speaker: Elizabeth
opening.text: Who that knows what his misfortunes have been can help feeling an interest in him?

opening.speaker: Mr. Darcy
opening.text: His misfortunes! yes, his misfortunes have been great indeed.
